output.myth: Ireth went north in the spring and south in the autumn, and never once asked anyone's leave. She flies from the ice at the pole to the warm grass of the south and back, which is more sea than any one bird should carry. Aun, the First Flier, once asked her how far the wind went, and she said, "Further than you, and I've been. Get out of my way." Mother Hesk counts the birds on her Reel every night, and every night Ireth is one short. The village makes its song for her and hangs her cloth on the cliff. Then, some grey morning when the cloth is nearly rotted, Ireth comes in low over the rocks, soaked, cross about the fog, and asks who has been eating her fish. Tavo laughs and blows her in. Nobody scolds her. Mend the net, the grandmothers say, and set out another bowl. The lost are not always dead. Some are only slow.
output.verse:
Ireth comes back wet
cross about the fog and late
set out one more bowl
